structure.title: Claim and mobilisation
structure.text: The early acts turn a disputed claim into preparations for invasion. Official arguments coexist with less exalted motives.

structure.title: Campaign and persuasion
structure.text: The French campaign tests leadership through speeches, threats, encounters with soldiers, and diplomatic negotiation.

people.name: Henry
people.text: The young king who claims the French throne and leads a small, sick, outnumbered English army across France.

people.name: The Chorus
people.text: A speaker who opens each act and begs the audience to let their imaginations fill a small wooden theatre with armies and oceans.

people.name: Common soldiers
people.text: Ordinary men in Henry's army, who talk in the night before the battle about what they owe their king, and what he owes them.

context.title: A claim to France
context.text: The invasion is justified through dynastic reasoning. The argument's complexity matters partly because it can authorise other people's danger.
context.takeaway: Ask who benefits from the interpretation.

context.title: Stage and imagination
context.text: The Chorus acknowledges the theatre's limited means. Its grand vision can differ from what subsequent scenes show.
context.takeaway: Compare the invitation with the performance.

notice.text: Listen for changes between public and private speech.
notice.why: Leadership involves different accounts for different audiences.
It creates solidarity without necessarily removing unequal risk.

opening: Henry needs his army to believe an invasion is worth dying for. He can make the argument magnificently, turning exhaustion and terrible odds into an invitation to belong to history. Shakespeare also takes him among soldiers who have less freedom to choose what this war means. The play allows the exhilaration of leadership its full force while leaving room for the threats, evasions, and bodies behind it. A king's ability to inspire becomes inseparable from his ability to decide whose suffering a victory will require.
